fields.subnational_unit: Same District, Kilimanjaro region (24 wards, 82 villages, 445 sub-villages)
fields.sample_size: Single-district action-research case (Same District, northeast Tanzania; rural population 207,800 in 2006 and 217,935 in 2009): district-wide water point mapping (WPM) baseline at the end of 2006 (598 water points) and a simplified village-level update in July 2009 (956 water points), a field study with interviews and meetings at district, ward and village levels, working sessions and seminars with district officials, and a review of 47 water-service actions implemented from July 2007 to June 2009 (37 by government, 10 by NGOs) and 22 planned for 2009-2011; the number of interviews is not reported
fields.effect_measure: descriptive indicators from district-wide water point mapping in 2006 and 2009 (coverage, functionality, equity, management) and an analysis of how projects were allocated; no inferential estimate
fields.effect_estimate: Between 2006 and 2009 358 water points were built (a 60% increase) but functionality stayed near 64% and coverage rose only from 65.06% to 68.76% of the national density threshold for improved water points, and from 43.37% to 46.78% for functional ones; redundant water points (in villages already above the threshold) rose from 22% to 33%, the Gini coefficient of coverage across villages fell only from 0.62 to 0.59 and villages without any improved water point fell from 20 to 7. The 47 actions of 2007-2009 reached 35 villages (the text says 35, Table 4 says 36), 47 villages received no support and 23 of the 46 villages with coverage below 25% were not targeted by any programme; the government's allocation was described as demand-driven but in practice 'cash driven' (cash contributions decided allocation) and politically influenced, and ward councillors and village leaders had little information on procedures or rights; only 11 of 82 villages collect regular tariffs and 61% have private connections. The authors built a planning framework (needs-based priority indices with a 25% coverage threshold, communication, awareness, supervision and a regular information system) and a District Water and Sanitation Unit Support (DWUS) for post-project support, arguing that the human-right-to-water frame helps local government target equity.
fields.section: Full text (journal article, 13 pages; scanned image PDF read page by page): 1. Introduction; 2. Water point mapping in Tanzania; 3. Methodology; 4. The evolution of water provision in Same District; 5. Analysis of results; 6. Framework for the improvement of planning; 7. Institutionalization of post-project support; 8. Conclusions
fields.risk_of_bias_rating: CASP Qualitative per-item (re-appraised 2026-10-09 on the full text; supersedes the abstract-only rating): 1(aims)=Yes; 2(qual approach)=Yes (action research suits an aim of building planning mechanisms with district stakeholders); 3(design)=Can't tell (the action-research design is named but not justified against alternatives); 4(recruitment)=Can't tell (district officials and village leaders were consulted; numbers and selection are not reported); 5(data collection)=Yes (district-wide water point mapping in 2006 and a village-level update in 2009, with interviews, meetings, working sessions and project records); 6(researcher-participant)=Can't tell (the authors worked with the implementing NGO and the district water department; the influence of that role on the findings is not discussed); 7(ethics)=Can't tell (not located); 8(analysis rigor)=Can't tell (descriptive tables and a list of conclusions; no analytic procedure for the qualitative material); 9(findings)=Yes; 10(value)=Yes. Per CASP's own guidance no composite score is computed.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: an action-research case in one Tanzanian district (2006-2009) with descriptive water point mapping indicators and an analysis of how projects were allocated; read in full text 2026-10-09.
